title: Fixed-subsheaf adjunctions and their normalized product comparison
statement:
Fix compatible universes [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $(C,J)$ be a small site with finite limits [def-weil-pbc-sites-and-cohomology], let $R$ be a sheaf of commutative unital rings, and let $K,L$ be sheaves of groups on $C$, with values in the coefficient universe. For a group sheaf $P$, write $\mathcal E_P(R)$ for sheaves of $R$-modules [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category] with restriction-natural operations $P(U)\times M(U)\to M(U)$ satisfying the group-action laws and linearity in $M(U)$, and equivariant linear maps, with sectionwise addition. Thus $\mathcal E_1(R)=\operatorname{Mod}(R)$. Inflation along a group-sheaf homomorphism means precomposition of actions, with the same modules and maps.

For $P=K,L,K\times L$, the submodules
$$M^P(U)=\{m\in M(U):\ \forall f:V\to U,\ \forall p\in P(V),\ p\cdot f^*m=f^*m\}$$
form an $R$-module subsheaf, naturally in $M$. For $M\in\mathcal E_{K\times L}(R)$ define $M^L$ by the same condition with $p=(1,l)$. It is a subsheaf carrying the restriction-natural residual $K$-action $k\cdot m=(k,1)\cdot m$. Restricting equivariant maps to these subsheaves defines additive functors $\Gamma_P:\mathcal E_P(R)\to\operatorname{Mod}(R)$ and $\Gamma_L^K:\mathcal E_{K\times L}(R)\to\mathcal E_K(R)$, with their sectionwise injective inclusions $i_P$ and $j_L$ into the underlying modules.

Let $T_P:\operatorname{Mod}(R)\to\mathcal E_P(R)$ give the trivial action and let $I:\mathcal E_K(R)\to\mathcal E_{K\times L}(R)$ inflate along the first projection. There are natural additive adjunctions $T_P\dashv\Gamma_P$ and $I\dashv\Gamma_L^K$ whose forward transposes keep every section map and restrict its codomain to the displayed invariant submodule, and whose inverse transposes compose with $i_P$, respectively $j_L$. In particular the adjunction for $I$ is $K$-equivariant for the specified residual action.

There is the identity comparison $T_{K\times L}=I\circ T_K$ of the trivial-action functors. Under the preceding normalized adjunctions, its conjugate right-adjoint comparison
$$c_M:M^{K\times L}\xrightarrow{\sim}(M^L)^K$$
is the identity on the underlying sections and is natural in $M$. Precisely, if $i_K:(M^L)^K\hookrightarrow M^L$ and $j_L:M^L\hookrightarrow M$ are the invariant inclusions, then $j_L\circ i_K\circ c_M=i_{K\times L}$ on every object of $C$; both sides include the same fixed section into $M$. All these statements hold when either group sheaf is trivial and when $R$ is the zero ring sheaf.

proof.text: For any group sheaf $P$ acting on $M$, denote the displayed subset by $F_P(U)$. It contains zero and is closed under addition, negatives and multiplication by $a\in R(U)$: for example, for $f:V\to U$ and $p\in P(V)$, $p\cdot f^*(am)=f^*a\,(p\cdot f^*m)=f^*a\,f^*m$. Here the first equality uses semilinearity of restrictions and linearity of the action. If $m\in F_P(U)$ and $g:W\to U$, then for every $h:V\to W$ the required equality for $g^*m$ is exactly the equality for $m$ along $gh$. Thus these submodules and the restrictions of $M$ form a module subpresheaf. Apply this also to the restricted $L$-action $(1,l)$ on a product-action module.

proof.text: Construct the family of fixed submodules as a module subpresheaf, and view it as a subfunctor of the underlying type-valued module presheaf. Apply Mathlib Subfunctor.isSheaf_iff: it suffices that locally fixed sections are fixed. For a locally fixed section m over U, a test arrow f:V→U and p∈P(V), pull back the covering sieve on which m is fixed. Along every arrow g:W→V in that pullback, the restriction of m is fixed. Naturality of the action and the fixedness condition tested at the identity of W show that g restricts p·f*m and f*m to the same section. Separatedness of M gives their equality. This works for arbitrary Grothendieck topologies, including empty covering sieves, without choosing fibre products or using sheafness of P.

proof.text:
For $m\in M^L(U)$ and $k\in K(U)$, take $f:V\to U$ and $l\in L(V)$. The two product factors commute, so
$$(1,l)\cdot f^*((k,1)\cdot m)=(1,l)\cdot((f^*k,1)\cdot f^*m)=(f^*k,1)\cdot((1,l)\cdot f^*m)=(f^*k,1)\cdot f^*m.$$
Thus $(k,1)\cdot m$ lies in $M^L(U)$. Its restriction-naturality, linearity, unit law and multiplication law are restrictions of those in $M$. The inclusion $j_L$ is $K$-equivariant by this formula. For an equivariant module map $a:M\to N$ and any fixed section $m$, one has $p\cdot f^*a(m)=a(p\cdot f^*m)=a(f^*m)$; hence $a$ restricts to the invariant subsheaves. Restricting identities and composites gives identities and composites; restricting $a+b$ gives the sum of the restrictions. This constructs the asserted additive functors $\Gamma_P$ and $\Gamma_L^K$, the latter with residual $K$-equivariant maps, and proves naturality of their inclusions.

proof.text:
Let $A\in\operatorname{Mod}(R)$ and $M\in\mathcal E_P(R)$. For an equivariant $a:T_PA\to M$ define $\Phi(a)_U(x)=a_U(x)$ with codomain $M^P(U)$. It lands there because for every $f:V\to U$ and $p\in P(V)$,
$$p\cdot f^*a_U(x)=p\cdot a_V(f^*x)=a_V(p\cdot f^*x)=a_V(f^*x).$$
The last equality uses the trivial action on $A$. The resulting component maps are linear and commute with restrictions because $a$ does. Conversely $b:A\to M^P$ gives $i_Pb:T_PA\to M$: equivariance follows by taking the identity restriction in the defining fixed-section condition. These operations are inverse, since neither changes any section value. For maps $u:A'\to A$ and equivariant $v:M\to M'$, both $\Phi(aT_Pu)=\Phi(a)u$ and $\Phi(va)=\Gamma_P(v)\Phi(a)$ hold on each section. They are additive, since $\Phi(a+a')$ and $\Phi(a)+\Phi(a')$ have section value $a_U(x)+a'_U(x)$. The natural-bijection adjunction theorem therefore gives the specified additive adjunction $T_P\dashv\Gamma_P$, whose counit is precisely $i_P$.

source.place: Tag 0037, definition-adjoint and following unit/counit formulas; direct construction of its Hom bijections for the item

proof.text:
For $A\in\mathcal E_K(R)$ and $M\in\mathcal E_{K\times L}(R)$, an equivariant $a:IA\to M$ has image in $M^L$: for $x\in A(U)$, $f:V\to U$ and $l\in L(V)$, $(1,l)\cdot f^*a(x)=a((1,l)\cdot f^*x)=a(f^*x)$. Define $\Psi(a)$ by restricting its codomain. It is $K$-equivariant since $a((k,1)\cdot x)=(k,1)\cdot a(x)$ and the source action is $k\cdot x$. Conversely a $K$-equivariant $b:A\to M^L$ gives $j_Lb:IA\to M$. For $(k,l)\in(K\times L)(U)$ its equivariance is the equality
$$(k,l)\cdot b(x)=(k,1)\cdot((1,l)\cdot b(x))=(k,1)\cdot b(x)=b(k\cdot x).$$
The maps are inverse on every section. Precomposition, postcomposition and sums preserve their formulas exactly as for $\Phi$ in step 4. The natural-bijection adjunction theorem gives $I\dashv\Gamma_L^K$ with counit $j_L$ and the required additive Hom bijections. Trivial action and inflation are themselves additive functors: on maps they keep each component linear map, its identities, composites and sums.

proof.text: The direct trivial-action functor and first-projection inflation after trivial action are definitionally equal on objects, morphisms and actions. Use reflexivity for their equality. The separate construction of an isomorphism from direct to successive invariant subsheaves is unnecessary: the actual conjugate isomorphism supplied by conjugateIsoEquiv already has its desired normalization by the next step.

proof.text: Instantiate Mathlib conjugateEquiv_counit with the direct fixed adjunction, the composite of the K-fixed and second-factor fixed adjunctions, and eqToIso of the inverse equality of trivial-action functors. Evaluate this equivariant morphism equality on each section x. By the explicit Hom-equivalence constructions, the direct counit is the direct invariant inclusion and the composite counit is the successive invariant inclusions. The equality comparison is an identity and both trivial action and inflation retain all underlying maps. The evaluated equation is definitionally the required section formula for conjugateIsoEquiv. Thus the displayed actual conjugate includes every section as its original value; no additional comparison or arbitrary witness is used. Trivial groups, zero coefficient rings and empty covers require no extra assumptions.
